overview: Sumer was a region of southern Mesopotamia, in modern Iraq, whose cities developed influential traditions of urban government, craftwork and writing. It was often divided among rival city-states. The atlas’s Sumer outline is displaced northwest of the actual heartland and misses Ur and Uruk. Its 4000 to 1500 BCE span covers several cultural and political phases, not one kingdom with unchanged borders.

periods.title: Cities and writing
periods.summary: Uruk expanded, and clay records developed for managing goods.

periods.title: Rival city-states
periods.summary: Separate ruling dynasties competed before Akkadian conquest.

periods.title: Empire and renewed local rule
periods.summary: Akkadian power eventually fragmented, allowing local dynasties to re-emerge.

periods.title: The Third Dynasty of Ur
periods.summary: Ur’s rulers united much of the region again.

periods.title: Successor kingdoms and scribal continuity
periods.summary: New rulers governed cities where Sumerian remained a language of learning.

items.text: Around 3200 BCE, Uruk’s monumental buildings used mud brick and walls decorated with coloured clay cones. Its earliest tablets recorded goods and workers’ rations with pictorial signs. Some of the beginnings of writing were practical bookkeeping: keeping track of supplies mattered in a growing city.

Sumer’s cities were frequently political rivals. Akkadian kings brought them under imperial control during the later third millennium BCE, but independent local rulers reappeared as that empire weakened. A single conquest did not permanently end the cities or their Sumerian traditions.

The later Third Dynasty of Ur left thousands of business documents and sponsored major building work. Ur-Nammu and his successors ruled a larger state centred on Ur. Administrative clay tablets are a less glittering discovery than jewellery, but they preserve exceptionally detailed evidence of how institutions handled resources.

Ur-Namma’s canal inscription describes digging a boundary channel dedicated to Nanna, extending it toward the sea and checking its course. The king presented water management as a duty to his god. Canals were engineered routes through the landscape, and their boundaries could also be politically sensitive.

sections.title: Food, work and a muddy paw print

items.text: A tablet from the temple of Bau at Girsu records barley for about two hundred workers and their children. Adults received thirty or forty sila per month, while children received twenty. It names a distribution under Uruinimgina in the twenty-fourth century BCE. Even children’s shares had to go into the accounts.

At Lagash, excavators identified a public eating place from around 2700 BCE. They found benches, an oven, storage vessels with food remains and a clay cooling installation. The interpretation suggests a place to prepare food and gather outside the home. No electricity was involved in this ancient effort to keep provisions cool.

Textile production around 2000 BCE involved women and children, with sheep’s wool turned into cloth and garments for exchange. Spindle whorls survive where most fabric has decayed. Making thread and weaving were major forms of labour behind the cities’ prosperity, not merely small finishing touches to palace life.

One brick from Ur carries both Ur-Nammu’s building inscription and a dog’s paw print. It was made around 2112 to 2095 BCE, and the animal stepped on the clay before it dried. The king recorded his achievements; the dog contributed an entirely different kind of signature.

By the third millennium BCE, goods could be valued in silver by weight, long before stamped coins. Merchants used scales and weights to compare payments. A shekel began as a weight unit: shopping and accounting did not require a pocket full of round coins.

In Ur’s later Old Babylonian neighbourhoods, around 1900 BCE, more than fifty houses stood along winding streets. Seals from one courtyard name Gimil-Ningizzida and his wife Ningal-lamazi. These personal traces belong to the city’s continuing life after Ur’s great dynasty ended, and let us identify a particular household.

Later scribal training at Nippur began with practising individual wedges and then combinations of signs. Students progressed to syllables, names and themed word lists. Learning Sumerian writing required both language study and physical skill: a reed pressed into clay behaved very differently from a pencil.

Some Nippur school tablets had a teacher’s example on one side of the front and a student’s repeatedly erased practice beside it. The practice area could become thin or break away. Clay made a reusable writing surface, although a determined learner could eventually wear out the homework.

A late-third-millennium tablet excavated at Nippur preserves medical prescriptions in Sumerian. Now catalogued as CBS 14221, it records an early effort to put treatment knowledge into writing. Its damaged surface also reminds us that surviving medical texts are incomplete evidence; this object cannot tell us how readily every family obtained care.

Game boards from Ur’s royal graves, around 2600 BCE, belong to the game now called Twenty Squares or the Royal Game of Ur. Versions travelled widely and later reached Egypt. A board game was portable entertainment as well as a crafted object; the excavated boards are older than surviving explanations of many rules.

A diorite statue of Gudea shows the ruler seated with folded hands. Its Sumerian inscription recounts temple building and dedicates the statue, intended to stand before a deity. The hard stone, carved robe and long text made worship, craftsmanship and royal self-presentation part of the same object.

Ur-Namma’s canal inscription includes “lugal urim₅ᵏⁱ-ma”, meaning “king of Urim”, or Ur. This is a scholarly Roman-letter transcription of the Sumerian cuneiform, preserved on cones from Girsu around 2100 BCE. The tiny raised “ki” marks a place-name in the transcription; it is not an extra spoken word.

ending.text: There was no single end to Sumer. Akkadian conquest changed its politics, and a later kingdom centred on Ur rose and collapsed around 2000 BCE amid attacks and competing powers. Isin, Larsa and Babylon became important successors. Sumerian continued in learned, religious and legal writing long after it ceased to be an everyday spoken language. The atlas’s 1500 BCE cutoff is not a disappearance date.
